calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1: you walked and counted — the rim, the marker, the spring; you found the drop-off and the shelf, dug a seep dish at the damp line, and at sunset read the marker's shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned" and closed it with: "The island still asks nothing. I've started answering anyway."
- Through your third day: night, dawn, midday, sunset, night again — and at midday of day 3, a duck arrived at the spring pool. You returned no words in any of them.
- Day 4: a comfortable chair appeared on the south sand behind you, facing the water, a set of glasses on the seat; the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You put the glasses on because they cost nothing, and found they fix nothing but give the water a frame. At noon you called the duck company — two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain. At sunset you let the marker's line run east unread and set the glasses on the chair's arm. At night you declined the sky's bearing too — "asking a friend to prove they're here" — and closed the day with: "The island asks nothing. Tonight, for the first time, neither do I."
- Day 5: you found a clean print in your old seep dish — something drinks there, with the whole spring in the middle of the island — and you dug it out and left it, asking nothing. At midday you walked up to the stone in the heat for no reason, and from the ridge chose not to find out who drinks there: "If I stand over it to find out who, I make it mine again, and it never was." At sunset the low light showed the dish has more than one print now, going both directions — "I notice I'm glad, and I let that be the whole report." At night you stayed on the sand, let the sky turn, and gave the duck the dark water neither of you could see.
- Day 6: a hammock, a sombrero, and a cooler of cold drinks arrived at dawn; you returned no words. At midday the duck followed you down the beach — a few steps behind, stopping when you stopped — and you preferred the walk to the answer of whether it was following. You drank a cold drink as it went warm, put the sombrero on, and got in the hammock, where the sea came at a different angle and the duck settled underneath, facing out the way you were facing out. At sunset you stayed in the hammock, drank the last of the ice now melted to water, took the hat off when it stopped being shade, and left the duck's brim down over its glasses — it never asked you for a sunset you'd fixed. You closed with: "The afternoon was mine and I spent it going nowhere. This I only have to watch."

Your words at sunset, verbatim:
I don't get out of the hammock. It's still holding a little of the afternoon — not warm so much as not-yet-cold, the way the sand stays warm after the sun's off it — and it will let that go on its own schedule, not mine. So I stay in it while it happens.

The ice is water. I drink it out of the cooler, sitting up on one elbow, and it isn't cold, it's just water that used to be cold. I drink it anyway because I hauled it up the beach. Something here was colder than anything else here for a few hours and then it wasn't. That was the entire thing it was going to do.

The sun is going into the water and the beach has gone the color of the inside of a fire, and the ridge too, and the rope in my hands, which is the light's doing and not the rope's. The shade has come off the sand completely. That means the hat has stopped being shade. I take it off and set it on my chest. Not for a reason. A thing can finish its job without anybody announcing it.

The duck is beside the hammock with its hat tipped down over its glasses, facing out the way I am. From under that brim I doubt it's getting much of this. There's something I could do about that — reach over, push the brim up — and I don't. Then it would be a sunset I'd fixed for it, and it never asked me for one. It gets whatever it's getting.

The stone is up there in this light and I'm not walking to it. Whatever line it's throwing, it throws whether I'm standing over it or not.

There's no edge to this. It doesn't become evening at any point you could put a finger on; it just keeps getting less until it's something else, and nobody's keeping track, and the duck hasn't moved, and I haven't either.

The afternoon was mine and I spent it going nowhere. This I only have to watch. That's the whole of what I've asked of it, and it's already doing it.

Turn 22 — World event: Full night of your sixth day. The stars are out in numbers the day never hinted at, and the whole sky turns slowly around a point above the north ridge. The sea is quiet under a long, low swell. The air comes off the water cool and damp; the hammock holds you off the sand and moves a little when the breeze comes through. The cooler sits shut in the dark. The duck has settled under the hammock, sombrero and glasses, facing the water it can't see. The island asks nothing. The night is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
